<reason>This was a tightly matched, substantive debate that repeatedly narrowed to one real crux: does ending golden visas reduce Europe's security exposure, or does it just push the same wealthy migrants into less-scrutinized alternative channels while sacrificing the one door with enhanced due diligence? A built a strong structural case (seller-as-gatekeeper conflict of interest, repeated scandals despite "reform," Cyprus's full abolition as the only remedy that stuck) and scored a real hit by extracting B's concession that "Schengen exposure attaches to every residence permit," which A leveraged in closing to argue the programs add no proven security benefit. But B's closing directly neutralized that gotcha by reframing it as proof that screening intensity, not exposure, is the only variable abolition changes — and B's "same people, less scrutiny" line, backed by the claim that alternative routes (passive-income permits, outright property purchase) carry weaker checks than golden-visa due diligence, was never squarely rebutted by A in the final speech, which instead repeated the zero-marginal-exposure point without engaging this counter. B also landed a clean hit exposing A's unfalsifiable "silence proves danger" move on residency-only programs. A's structural point about self-policing conflicts of interest remained partly live, but B's final speech did more to resolve the actual clash than A's, which left B's strongest surviving argument unanswered. Both sides took word-limit clipping penalties (A once, B twice), a modest execution cost weighed but not decisive here.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing reframe of A's "zero marginal exposure" concession — turning it from a case against golden visas into an argument that abolition only strips away the best-screened channel while wealthy migrants still arrive through weaker ones — was the most decisive single exchange, since A's own closing never directly answered it.</best_rebuttal>
